stories.headline: S&P 500, NASDAQ-100 SLIDE AS AI-REVENUE DOUBTS HIT MEGA-CAP TECH
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.47% to 7,765 and the Nasdaq-100 dropped 1.39% to 30,726 after a Financial Times report cast doubt on OpenAI's revenue trajectory, dragging Nvidia, Micron, and Intel lower; the Dow Jones bucked the trend, adding roughly 0.1% as money rotated into value names outside the AI trade. Markets are closed for the weekend with no new catalyst to move these levels.
stories.explain: Mega-cap AI suppliers trade on a long-duration growth story: today's price embeds years of assumed compute demand from a small number of customers, chief among them OpenAI, so any doubt about that demand materializing resets the present value of distant cash flows disproportionately hard. The Dow's gain while the Nasdaq-100 fell shows the selling is concentrated rotation out of AI-exposed names rather than a broad risk-off move, which matters because the two patterns call for very different responses from investors.

stories.headline: OIL CLIMBS ON REPORTS OF POTENTIAL U.S. STRIKES ON IRAN AS 10-YEAR YIELD HOLDS NEAR 2007 HIGHS
stories.body: WTI crude rose 1.26% to roughly $91 a barrel after reports that the Pentagon is preparing contingency options for potential military action against Iran, while the 10-year Treasury yield eased 5 basis points to 5.23% but remains close to its highest level since 2007. No fresh de-escalation or escalation headlines broke over the weekend.
stories.explain: Oil's move is a geopolitical risk premium, not a demand story: traders price in the probability that an escalation could disrupt tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, so the barrel price rises even before any actual supply is lost. The 10-year's stickiness near 5.2% compounds the tech selloff because it raises the discount rate applied to exactly the kind of long-duration cash flows the AI trade depends on, so elevated yields and AI-revenue doubts are pulling on the same valuation lever from different directions.

stories.headline: GOVERNMENT FUNDED THROUGH DEC. 11 AS FY27 APPROPRIATIONS FIGHT STALLS IN THE SENATE
stories.body: The government remains funded through December 11 under the continuing resolution President Trump signed September 2 (House vote: 370-48), but none of the twelve FY2027 appropriations bills have yet been taken up by the Senate Appropriations Committee, setting up a funding cliff just after the midterm elections.
stories.explain: A continuing resolution freezes spending at prior-year levels rather than passing new appropriations, which avoids an immediate shutdown but pushes the harder fights over specific agency funding levels down the calendar. Punting the fight to right after the midterms raises the stakes because the incoming Congress's composition could change the bargaining leverage on both sides, and unresolved appropriations uncertainty is itself a small drag on Treasury issuance planning and the term premium investors demand for holding long bonds.

stories.headline: DOLLAR DIPS, GOLD HOLDS NEAR $4,160 AS HAVEN DEMAND NETS OUT FLAT
stories.body: The DXY slipped 0.11% to 102.11 while gold held essentially flat near $4,160 an ounce, as safe-haven demand tied to the Iran headlines roughly offset the dollar's own modest pullback. Both figures carry over unchanged into the weekend since currency and metals desks are quiet until Monday.
stories.explain: Gold and the dollar are both haven assets that usually move in opposite directions because gold is priced in dollars, so a weaker dollar should mechanically lift gold's price for dollar-based buyers. The flat gold price despite the softer dollar suggests the geopolitical bid for gold specifically is roughly balanced against reduced haven demand for the dollar itself, a sign investors aren't yet treating the Iran headlines as a major escalation.

stories.headline: KANSAS'S TYRAN STOKES, ARKANSAS'S JORDAN SMITH JR. HEADLINE PRESEASON ALL-AMERICA BUZZ AHEAD OF NOV. 2 TIP-OFF
stories.body: Five-star freshmen Tyran Stokes (Kansas) and Jordan Smith Jr. (Arkansas) are drawing early preseason All-America attention as outlets release first Top 25 projections, with BartTorvik's model slotting Kansas at No. 10 nationally. St. John's continues reshaping its rotation around guard Donnie Freeman's season-ending Achilles injury as Big East play approaches in November.

stories.headline: GIANNIS'S HEAT OFFENSE KEEPS CLICKING IN PRESEASON AS LEAGUE SETS OCT. 20 OPENING NIGHT
stories.body: Giannis Antetokounmpo scored 18 points on 8-of-13 shooting in Miami's 128-118 preseason win over New Orleans, extending a strong start to his post-Milwaukee debut after the trade that sent Tyler Herro north. The league's Oct. 20 opening night is set: the champion Knicks host LeBron James and the 76ers for New York's ring ceremony, while Detroit opens at home against Boston.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS HOST UNBEATEN 49ERS SUNDAY WITH FIRST PLACE IN THE NFC WEST ON THE LINE
stories.body: Seattle (3-1) and San Francisco kicked off at 4:25 p.m. ET at Lumen Field, with Seattle favored by roughly 3 points behind the league's top-ranked defensive DVOA against a 49ers offense missing Nick Bosa (knee/calf). The game was still in progress as this brief was published; check back for the final.

stories.headline: NO. 1 TEXAS STUNNED BY OKLAHOMA 27-24 ON WALK-OFF FIELD GOAL AS GEORGIA TOPPLES BAMA IN TUSCALOOSA
stories.body: Tate Sandell's 47-yard field goal on the final play gave Oklahoma a 27-24 upset of top-ranked Texas in the 122nd Red River Rivalry at the Cotton Bowl, the Sooners' first win in the series since 2023 and the Longhorns' first loss of the season. Hours earlier, No. 2 Georgia beat No. 6 Alabama 20-17 at Bryant-Denny Stadium behind Gunner Stockton's two touchdowns — Georgia's first regular-season win there since 2007 — setting up a likely move to No. 1 in Monday's poll.

sports.detail: Fell to No. 20 Iowa 41-24 at Husky Stadium Friday night, trailing 27-0 at halftime as Kamari Moulton ran for a career-high 208 yards and two touchdowns; UW's rushing attack was held to -3 yards. Washington drops to 3-3 (0-3 Big Ten). Next: at Purdue, Friday, Oct. 16, 5 p.m. PT (FOX) — UW's first trip to Purdue since 1990 — before a bye week Oct. 24.

UW continues preparing its 2026-27 roster, with nine new players competing for roles after losing top scorers Hannes Steinbach (NBA Draft, Charlotte) and Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky). Next: exhibition at Boise State, Saturday, Oct. 17, 7 p.m. MT (Idaho Central Arena), then hosts rival Washington State Oct. 25 before opening the regular season at home vs. Colgate Nov. 2 and returning to the Maui Invitational Nov. 23 vs. BYU.

Hosting unbeaten San Francisco today at Lumen Field with first place in the NFC West on the line; kickoff was 4:25 p.m. ET and the game was still in progress as this brief published. Seattle enters 3-1 after last week's 30-23 win over the Chargers, with Sam Darnold up to No. 21 in the NFL's Top 100 rankings.

Center Jalen Duren, who signed a fully guaranteed five-year, $200 million deal Oct. 2, remains in camp as the roster rounds into form. Next: regular-season opener Oct. 20 vs. Boston, part of the NBA's nationally televised opening night.

Finished the season 76-86, missing the playoffs for the first time since 2019 after last year's Game 7 ALCS run. The managerial search is ongoing with no hire yet; president of baseball ops Jerry Dipoto says the club will look outside the organization, with Torey Lovullo off the board after re-signing with Arizona and commentators noting Seattle's below-market managerial pay as a possible deterrent to candidates. deepDive.title: Oil's War Premium: How a Naval Blockade Shows Up in the Brent-WTI Spread
content: Today's brief carries over a detail worth sitting with: WTI near $92 a barrel, moving on reports that the Pentagon is weighing further options against Iran rather than on any actual change in the physical supply of oil. That framing — price moving before barrels move — is the whole story of how a geopolitical risk premium gets built into energy markets, and it's especially visible right now because the U.S. has had an active naval posture around Iranian shipping for months. For a finance student, the more revealing number isn't WTI alone, it's the spread between WTI and Brent, the two benchmark crudes that normally track each other closely but diverge sharply when a specific geography is threatened.

WTI is a landlocked U.S. benchmark priced off storage at Cushing, Oklahoma, largely insulated from seaborne chokepoints. Brent is a waterborne benchmark for crude that physically has to pass by or near conflict zones, including the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global oil consumption flows. When the threat of a blockade or strikes rises, Brent typically bids up faster and higher than WTI because the risk is specifically to seaborne cargo, widening the Brent-WTI spread even if headline WTI is also rising in sympathy. Options markets confirm this isn't guesswork: Brent options skew showed call demand spiking on blockade headlines, a direct read on traders pricing upside tail risk, not expected demand growth.

What most casual market-watchers miss is that the spread, not the price level, is the cleaner signal of how seriously traders take an escalation. During the 1990 Gulf War buildup, Brent-WTI spreads swung by several dollars within weeks even before a shot was fired, because tanker insurance and freight rates in the Gulf repriced ahead of any actual seizure. The same logic applies today: a widening spread alongside a steepening Brent forward curve into backwardation — near-term contracts pricing above later-dated ones — tells you the market expects a supply disruption soon, not eventually, which is a materially different signal than a parallel rise in both benchmarks that reflects generic risk-off sentiment.

The read-through for a portfolio sitting next to this brief's other story about a 10-year yield stuck near 2007 highs: oil's war premium feeds directly into headline CPI, and a sustained spike raises the odds the Fed holds rates higher for longer, reinforcing exactly the discount-rate pressure already weighing on long-duration growth stocks. Watch the Brent-WTI spread, not just the WTI print, over the coming week — a spread that keeps widening even as WTI itself is flat would be the tell that traders expect the Hormuz risk to escalate rather than fade, with knock-on effects for inflation expectations, the term premium, and the AI-trade valuations already under pressure in today's macro story.
